title: Arm Regeneration Masters
quote: These sea stars can drop off an arm and from it, it will regrow a complete animal. ... Instead of looking like stars, they often look like comets. From the “tail” of the comet, the arm that was dropped off, 4 arms are slowly growing back to form a new complete sea star. As the process continues, the little arms grow bigger, and they will eventually end up looking like stars again. ... If many species of sea stars can regrow a missing arm, only a few can, like Linckia multifora, regrow a full animal from just an arm.
newFact: Most sea stars can regrow a lost arm, but the comet star Linckia multifora can drop an arm and grow a whole new animal from it! Four tiny arms sprout from the dropped one, so for a while it looks like a comet. As those arms grow, it turns back into a star.
note: Whole body from one arm narrowed to a few species like Linckia, with the source's comet stage added; split-in-half claim dropped (second point, source mentions splitting only for flatworms).

title: Spit Happens
publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
quote: Alpacas rarely spit at people unless frightened or abused, but will use this form of communication with each other to register a complaint. ... Alpacas are social herd animals, and their only defense is flight.
newFact: Alpacas rarely spit at people unless they're frightened or mistreated. Spitting is mostly alpaca-to-alpaca talk: it's how one alpaca files a complaint with another! It isn't their big defense move, either. When real danger shows up, an alpaca's only defense is to run.
note: 'Main defense' replaced with spit as a complaint between alpacas (only defense is flight); food competition and 10-foot range dropped (only forums and owner sites found).

title: Underwater Makeover
quote: Most of its body is a clear gel almost the same density as the water around it. ... Their comedic melting in air isn't because of the loss of pressure, although the cold and pressure at depth likely keeps the gel firmer, but because the support given by water has been removed. Gravity then takes over causing the gel-layer just under the skin to make its way down. ... The lips sag into a frown, a fold of skin flops forward forming a drooping nose, and an icon is born. ... Photographed in their proper environment, blobfish are more like tadpoles on steroids, sometimes with striking patterns and frills.
newFact: The blobfish only looks like a sad blob out of water! Its body is mostly gel about as dense as seawater, so the water holds it up. Without that support, gravity drags the gel down: the lips sag into a frown and a skin fold flops into a droopy nose. Deep down, it's more like a tadpole on steroids.
note: Pressure swapped for the water's support; big nose moved to out of water only; deep-sea look is now 'tadpole on steroids'.

title: The Big Heart Myth
publisher: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance Library
quote: An early study (Goetz 1955) reported a very large (11.25 kg) heart for giraffes, but this may have been an error in measurement. A comprehensive study of the giraffe cardiovascular system (Mitchell and Skinner 2009) showed heart size relative to body mass to be comparable to that of other mammals. ... As a giraffe grows, the left ventricular and interventricular walls become much thicker than in other mammals, enabling the heart to contract much more strongly. ... Giraffes are up to 18 feet tall ... High blood pressure helps maintain sufficient blood flow to the brain. ... Systemic blood pressure at the heart with the neck held 55° to the vertical is calculated to be 208 mm Hg, nearly twice the predicted value for other species of similar size.
newFact: A 1955 study said giraffe hearts weigh about 25 pounds (11 kg), but it was probably a measuring mistake. The heart is actually normal-sized for the body. Its real trick is extra-thick walls that squeeze hard, pushing blood pressure to nearly twice that of similar-sized mammals so blood reaches the brain of an 18-foot-tall animal.
note: Blood pressure now compared with similar-sized mammals, not humans, and tied to the thick heart walls; unsupported 6-foot neck replaced with the page's 18 feet tall.

title: The Wave of Peace
quote: Submission is signalled by waving the forearm, which generally defuses the confrontation ... Arm waving is used by both sexes; males use waving to show submission to a dominant male
newFact: Bearded dragons wave a front leg to say 'no threat here!' When a male faces off with a dominant male, he waves his forearm to show submission, and that usually defuses the standoff before it turns into a fight. It's a scaly little white flag.
note: 'Polite greeting' dropped; wave is now submission that defuses fights. Female responsiveness wave cut as a second point.

title: Unique Nose Prints
quote: This paper shows that the canine nose pattern, which is an interlocking pattern of beads and grooves on a dog's nose, is unique to each individual dog. ... It was found that the canine nose pattern remains invariant regardless of when the image is taken ... the most well-known example is that of the Canadian Kennel Club accepting canine nose prints as proof of identity since 1938. What was to be presented to the Canadian Kennel Club was the actual print of a dog's nose (nose print) imprinted on a paper with ink.
newFact: Every dog's nose has its own pattern of tiny bumps and grooves, and it stays the same over time: a true doggy fingerprint! Nose print ID isn't new, either. Since 1938, the Canadian Kennel Club has accepted inked nose prints as proof of a dog's identity.
note: 'Have started using' replaced with the Canadian Kennel Club's use since 1938; added the beads-and-grooves pattern that stays the same over time.

title: Dogs Dream Too
publisher: Texas A&M College of Veterinary Medicine
quote: However, we will never really know if pets dream because we cannot talk to them. However, we do know that dogs have the REM sleep phase and this is the dream activity period in people. Dogs do have leg movements, facial twitching, vocalizations, and tail movements. Therefore, it might be likely they are having a dream.
quote2: But the structure of their sleep looks remarkably human: Like humans, dogs cycle through stages of wakefulness, rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep and non-rapid-eye-movement sleep. ... "What we've basically found is that dogs dream doggy things," Coren said. "So, pointers will point at dream birds, and Dobermans will chase dream burglars."
newFact: Dogs probably dream! Their sleep looks remarkably human, with REM, the stage when people dream. That's when you'll see twitching legs, wagging tails and little noises. Dogs can't tell us for sure, but one expert says they dream doggy things: pointers point at dream birds, and Dobermans chase dream burglars.
note: 'Just like humans' softened to 'probably'; 'remarkably similar' saved via Live Science; 'relive their day' dropped (shown only in rats) and replaced with Coren's doggy-dreams line.

title: Born Blind and Deaf
quote: Sensory function in neonatal dogs and cats is primarily tactile, olfactory and gustatory. The visual and auditory senses, although partially functional at birth, exhibit significant postnatal development: in the dog, the eyes do not open until a puppy is 8 to 10 days of age, the ear canals do not open until it is 12 to 13 days of age, and mature system function up through the cortex is not present until it is 3 months of age or older.
newFact: Newborn puppies get around mostly by touch, smell and taste! Their eyes and ears work only a little at birth. A puppy's eyes don't open until about 8 to 10 days old, and its ear canals open at 12 to 13 days. Fully grown-up sight and hearing take 3 months or more.
note: 'Completely blind and deaf' and 'entirely smell and touch' corrected to partial senses plus touch, smell and taste; eye opening 8 to 10 days, ears 12 to 13; title changed.

title: Meow is Just for Us
quote: A vocalization that seems to have particularly been affected by the domestication is the meow, notably used to attract human attention. As explained above, the meow is a rare vocalization in cat-cat interactions but is one of the most common vocalizations in cat-human interactions. ... Instead of creating new vocalization types, it is more probable that the cat has modified the function of some of its vocalizations to communicate adequately with humans. ... The feral cats produce almost no meow in the presence of a caretaker, but the rate can increase to resemble those of the house cats after regular contact with a human caretaker over a period of weeks.
newFact: Cats rarely meow at each other, yet the meow is one of their most common sounds around people! Researchers think cats didn't invent it for us: they repurposed an old call to get our attention. Feral cats barely meow at a caretaker at first, then meow more after weeks of regular contact.
note: 'Only at humans' softened to rare between cats; 'invented' replaced with repurposed; feral-cat detail added; unique vocabulary dropped (source notes only individual variation).
